title: Thomas Cook Collapse: Who Paid to Fly 140,000 Home?
summary:
Thomas Cook's collapse explained from the National Audit Office report: who paid to fly 140,000 stranded holidaymakers home, and why the government funded the rescue but refused the bailout.

On 23 September 2019 one of the world's oldest travel firms went into compulsory liquidation. Using the NAO's March 2020 investigation, the Commons business committee's questioning of chief executive Peter Fankhauser, Hansard, the company's own stock-exchange announcements, the CAA's annual report and the FRC's 2025 sanctions against auditor EY, we follow the debt, the final weekend, Operation Matterhorn and the estimated £83 million bill that fell on the taxpayer. Quotes are those of the people and bodies cited; 'Our analysis' is labelled as our own reading.

scenes.say: Chapter one. The oldest name in travel. How did a firm that pioneered package tours end up owing billions?

visual.text: The oldest name in travel

scenes.say: It began on the fifth of July, eighteen forty-one, with a train from Leicester to Loughborough.

visual.text: Thomas Cook's charter train: Leicester to Loughborough

scenes.say: Thomas Cook chartered it for four hundred and eighty-five temperance society members, at one shilling each.

visual.title: The birth of the travel guide
lines: A charter train from Leicester to Loughborough

scenes.say: A hundred and seventy-eight years later, the name was on high-street shops, hotels and its own airline. It had sent Britons on holiday for generations.

visual.label: years old when it collapsed
visual.sub: as the committee chair put it to the company's chairman

scenes.say: Its chief executive from twenty fourteen was Peter Fankhauser. He is the man MPs would later question about what he knew, and what he was paid.

visual.text: Peter Fankhauser
visual.sub: CEO from 2014, as an MP put it to him

scenes.say: To MPs, he named the weight the business carried.

visual.text: The debt

scenes.say: Since twenty twelve, he said, the group had paid one point two billion pounds in interest and refinancing costs.

visual.text: Since 2012, we paid £1.2 billion of interest costs and refinancing costs.

scenes.say: The company's chairman dated the trouble further back, to a merger.

visual.text: Thomas Cook merges with MyTravel

scenes.say: It basically all started, Frank Meysman told MPs, in two thousand and seven, with the merger with MyTravel.

visual.text: It basically all started in 2007 with the acquisition and merger with MyTravel.

scenes.say: Chapter two. The warning signs. When did the government start planning for a collapse?

visual.text: The warning signs

scenes.say: In May twenty nineteen, Thomas Cook reported a half-year loss before tax of one point four six billion pounds.
Most of it was a write-down of one point one billion pounds in the UK business, tied to the MyTravel merger twelve years earlier. The old deal was finally being priced in.
Net debt stood at one point two five billion.
The aviation regulator had already stepped up its monitoring, in September twenty eighteen.

visual.text: CAA steps up monitoring of Thomas Cook

scenes.say: And by April twenty nineteen, the Department for Transport was contingency planning with it.

visual.text: DfT and the CAA begin contingency planning

scenes.say: So the government had months to prepare for the worst. The question was whether the company could avoid it. Its answer was a new owner.
Chapter three. The rescue deal. Thomas Cook had a buyer lined up. Why wasn't it enough?

visual.text: The rescue deal

scenes.say: On the twenty-eighth of August, the company announced substantial agreement on a recapitalisation.
China's Fosun would put in four hundred and fifty million pounds of new money.

visual.label: new money from Fosun
visual.sub: for at least 75% of the tour operator and 25% of the airline

scenes.say: Banks and bondholders were to bring roughly the same again, about nine hundred million in total.
Then, in the final weeks, the lenders asked for more. An extra two hundred million pounds, on top of the deal already agreed.

visual.label: extra demanded at the last minute

scenes.say: Fankhauser told MPs the company heavily disputed the need for it.

visual.text: We heavily disputed the need for the £200 million...

scenes.say: The lenders, he said, wanted a backstop, in case everything went wrong.

visual.text: a cover as a backstop security, in case everything goes wrong

scenes.say: To close the gap, Thomas Cook turned to the government.

visual.text: A request for support
visual.sub: Thomas Cook writes to the government

scenes.say: Chapter four. The final weekend. Who made the call, and when did Fankhauser know?

visual.text: The final weekend

scenes.say: According to the National Audit Office, the request was for the government to guarantee a hundred and fifty to two hundred and fifty million pounds of loans.
Figures differ. The Prime Minister spoke of about a hundred and fifty million.

visual.text: ...a request was made to the Government for a subvention of about £150 million.

scenes.say: But the rescue plan was already settled. Treasury and the Prime Minister had approved it the day before the request.
On the eighteenth, the Transport Secretary confirmed he would reimburse the regulator's costs for customers without ATOL protection, whether Thomas Cook ultimately collapsed or not.

visual.title: 18 September 2019
lines: Transport Secretary to reimburse CAA costs
!whether Thomas Cook ultimately collapsed or not

scenes.say: On Sunday the twenty-second, the Department for Transport turned the request down.

visual.text: DfT refuses Thomas Cook's request

scenes.say: Meysman told MPs the decisive meeting was at four o'clock on that famous Sunday.

visual.text: at 4 o'clock on that famous Sunday

scenes.say: About an hour later, Fankhauser got a call from a senior official.

visual.text: A call from a senior official

scenes.say: He told MPs: I knew that I had to throw in the towel. He also said the company's own estimate of what a collapse would cost was far higher than what it had asked for.

visual.text: I knew that I had to throw in the towel.

scenes.say: At around two in the morning on Monday, the directors applied for compulsory liquidation.

visual.text: Directors file for compulsory liquidation

scenes.say: The board said it had no choice. Fankhauser called it a matter of profound regret.

visual.title: Compulsory liquidation
lines: had no choice but to take steps to enter into compulsory liquidation

scenes.say: Chapter five. Operation Matterhorn. How do you fly home a small city's worth of people in two weeks?

visual.text: Operation Matterhorn

scenes.say: The Transport Secretary called it the biggest peacetime repatriation in UK history.

visual.text: the biggest peacetime repatriation in UK history

scenes.say: Between the twenty-third of September and the seventh of October, more than a hundred and forty thousand people were flown home.
Seven hundred and forty-six flights, from fifty-four airports in eighteen countries. The regulator says its teams contacted all three thousand Thomas Cook hotels.
The regulator used a hundred and fifty aircraft from fifty partners.
Ninety-four per cent got home on their original date.

visual.label: home on their original return date

scenes.say: The Ministry of Defence put its Voyager jets at about twenty-seven million pounds for three aircraft for a month. The department judged that not cost-effective.

visual.title: The RAF option
lines: !approximately £27 million for three aircraft for one month

scenes.say: And the grounding of the Boeing 737 MAX meant fewer spare planes to hire.
Chapter six. Who paid. The flights were free for the passengers. So whose money was it?

visual.text: Who paid

scenes.say: The auditors estimated the repatriation cost at a hundred and fifty-two million pounds.
Customers with ATOL protection were covered by the Air Travel Trust Fund. It paid about sixty-nine million.

visual.title: Who paid for the flights home

scenes.say: Everyone else had no ATOL protection. For them, the Department for Transport expected to pay an estimated eighty-three million pounds. Fifty-five per cent.
That share grew. The regulator first estimated forty per cent of customers lacked protection. Booking data showed fifty-five.
The difference added about twenty-two million pounds to the taxpayer's bill. The real mix only became clear from booking data in January and February twenty twenty.

visual.label: added by the higher non-ATOL share

scenes.say: Add at least fifty-eight million in redundancy payments, and the Official Receiver's costs, and the government's known bill passed a hundred and fifty-six million.

visual.title: Known cost to government: at least £156m

scenes.say: The trust fund faced a far larger call: an estimated four hundred and eighty-one million pounds, mostly refunds.
By March twenty twenty, ATOL had resolved three hundred and thirty-five thousand claims and paid three hundred and forty-five million pounds, the most in the scheme's history.

visual.label: ATOL refunds paid by 31 March 2020
visual.sub: the largest amount the scheme had ever paid out

scenes.say: The department asked banks, insurers and the travel trade to chip in. After Monarch's collapse, it had recovered just two point three million of forty-five.
Then came injury claims. The Business Secretary wrote that Thomas Cook only insured itself against the very largest.

visual.text: This is an extraordinary situation which should never have arisen.

scenes.say: Chapter seven. Before the MPs. Would the chief executive give anything back?

visual.text: Before the MPs

scenes.say: On the fifteenth of October, Fankhauser faced the business committee. He opened with an apology.

visual.text: I am deeply sorry about this failure.

scenes.say: He said he got no bonus for twenty eighteen or twenty nineteen.

visual.text: I did not get a bonus for 2018, or for 2019 of course.

scenes.say: His twenty seventeen bonus, he said, was about seven hundred and fifty thousand pounds, thirty per cent in shares.

visual.label: his 2017 bonus, as he described it

scenes.say: The chair, Rachel Reeves, cited twenty million pounds in board bonuses over five years.

visual.label: board bonuses over five years, as the chair put it

scenes.say: Asked if he would hand money back, he said he would consider what was right, but not decide that day.

visual.text: I will consider what is right, but I am not going to decide that today.

scenes.say: Reeves replied that his apologies rang rather hollow. Later, she told the chairman, Frank Meysman, that the board had brought down a hundred and seventy-eight-year-old business, with huge repercussions for customers, staff and taxpayers.

visual.text: The number of times you have said 'sorry' rings rather hollow when you are not willing to put something back.

scenes.say: He told MPs he did not set his pay, and had not sold one share. Shares worth about four million pounds from an incentive plan were, he said, now worthless.

visual.title: Fankhauser, on his pay
items: "I am not the one who is setting my pay"
No 2% pay rise in April 2019, he said

scenes.say: On the refusal, he said the government did not want to create a precedent.

visual.text: They did not want to create a precedent to support the business.

scenes.say: Our analysis. So why pay for the flights but not the firm? Here is what ministers said.

visual.text: Our analysis

scenes.say: Two days after the collapse, Grant Shapps told the Commons a bailout risked throwing good money after bad. He pointed to the one point five billion pound half-year loss.

visual.text: we would risk throwing away good money after bad

scenes.say: He said there was no guarantee an injection would have saved the company, and an accounting officer would not have signed it off.

visual.title: The government's reasons
items: No guarantee it would save the company
An accounting officer would not sign it off
Moral hazard, said the Prime Minister

scenes.say: Germany did lend to Thomas Cook's German airline, Condor. Shapps said Condor's business remained profitable.

visual.text: With Condor, the business remained profitable.

scenes.say: Our reading: the flights were a pre-planned, bounded cost the state had prepared for since April. The bailout came with no guarantee.
The audit office itself made no judgement on whether refusing was right. And the Official Receiver's report on the directors' conduct, it noted, will not be made public.
About nine thousand UK staff lost their jobs. The Official Receiver estimated liabilities at around nine billion pounds.
Hays Travel bought all five hundred and fifty-five UK shops. Fosun bought the brand for eleven million pounds.
The Insolvency Service said in twenty twenty-two it did not intend to bring disqualification proceedings against the directors.

visual.text: No disqualification proceedings against the directors, as reported

scenes.say: And in April twenty twenty-five, the accounting watchdog fined auditor EY over its Thomas Cook audits, on goodwill, going concern and independence. It did not find the breaches intentional or reckless, or the accounts misstated.

visual.title: Sanctions against EY
lines: Thomas Cook audits, FY2017 and FY2018

scenes.say: The verdict: the taxpayer paid an estimated eighty-three million pounds to fly people home, and, as of January twenty twenty-two, the Insolvency Service did not intend to bring disqualification proceedings against the directors.
For another case where the auditor was fined after the collapse, watch our Patisserie Valerie episode.
